# @fivexer/agent

Run AI agents on your own machines as Fivexer workers.

Fivexer routes work to whoever fits — by tags, skills, priority, SLA and escalation. This daemon
makes a local agent CLI one of those candidates. Someone asks for an SEO audit through the Fivexer
MCP server, the matcher picks the worker that fits, and if that worker is an agent on your laptop,
this is what picks the task up, runs it, and reports back.

**Vendor-neutral by construction.** The daemon spawns a command and reads a JSON file. That works
with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cline, Goose, Aider — or a `#!/bin/sh` script, which is what the
test suite runs against. Nothing here depends on any vendor's protocol.

Capability stays on your host: your MCP servers, your API keys, your browser, your filesystem.
Routing, SLA, escalation and learning stay in Fivexer.

## Quick start

On a machine you are sitting at:

```bash
npx @fivexer/agent init          # opens your browser to sign in
npx @fivexer/agent doctor        # check everything before a task depends on it
npx @fivexer/agent run
```

`init` finds which agent CLIs you already have, asks which should do the work, where it should work
and what it may do, signs you in through the browser, registers the worker and puts it on shift.
Nothing to copy, nothing to paste. At a terminal the questions are lists — arrow keys to move, Space
to tick, Enter to confirm, Ctrl-C to stop with nothing registered; in a script each is a flag.

If the sign-in cannot get through — no browser, a proxy, a self-hosted deployment at another
address — it asks for a join link instead rather than making you start over. `--base-url` points it
at a deployment other than `https://api.5xer.com`.

### On a machine you are not sitting at

A server, a container, anything without a browser. In the console, open **Agents → Connect an
agent**, say who it is for (the whole workspace, or one person's assistant), name it and type what it
can do. You get one line to run on the machine:

```bash
npx -y @fivexer/agent init --join 'https://api.5xer.com/v1/worker-auth/join?token=jl_…' && npx -y @fivexer/agent run
```

The console page watches the link and says when the agent is online. A worker can do the same for
their own assistant from the portal (Me → My AI assistant). An assistant only takes work handed to it
on its owner's behalf, never the shared queue.

For a host meant to keep running, install it instead:

```bash
npm install -g @fivexer/agent
fivexer-agent init --yes --executor claude \
  --join 'https://api.5xer.com/v1/worker-auth/join?token=jl_…'
fivexer-agent service install    # writes a service unit; does not enable it
```

Install it rather than `npx` it on a host meant to keep running — see
[Running in production](#running-in-production).

The link is scoped to creating one worker, so it is the right thing to put in a provisioning
script. The browser flow is skipped automatically when a link is supplied; `--no-web` forces it off.

For a fleet you would rather drive from a workspace key: `init --api-key sk_… --workspace-id ws_…
--tags agent,research`.

**No long-lived workspace credential ever lands on the host.** Whichever path you take, what stays
on disk is a `wt_` worker session that reaches only its own queue, plus a PIN to renew it. The
browser token and the API key are both used once and dropped.

## Commands

|                   |                                                                       |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `init`            | set this machine up: pick an agent, register, scaffold its home       |
| `join <link>`     | register a profile by redeeming a join link                           |
| `doctor`          | check config, credentials, executors and shift state; claims nothing  |
| `profile <name>`  | show or change what a profile may do, after `init`                    |
| `run`             | work every profile's queue until stopped                              |
| `once`            | one pass over every queue, then exit — for cron, or a smoke test      |
| `next`            | print the next task and exit                                          |
| `mcp`             | speak MCP over stdio, so an interactive agent pulls its own work      |
| `service install` | write a user-level systemd / launchd / Scheduled Task unit, unenabled |

`--config <path>` picks a config file; `--profile <name>` narrows any command to one profile.

## Bringing your own agent

`init` creates `~/.fivexer/agents/<profile>/` and runs the agent there. That directory is yours:

```
~/.fivexer/agents/research/
  AGENTS.md        # standing instructions for every task this agent handles
  .mcp.json        # this agent's own MCP servers — its capabilities
  .claude/skills/  # Claude Code skills, when that is the executor
  README.md        # generated: where your chosen CLI reads each of these from
```

Fivexer never reads it. Put your MCP servers, your instructions and your skills there and they
apply to every task this profile is routed.

### Running it in your own project, with your permissions

The agent home is the safe default, not the only choice. To have the agent work the way it does
when you run it yourself — your project's skills, `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md`, `.mcp.json` and
settings — run it in that project. `init` started inside a project offers it; otherwise pass the
flags (they work on `join` too):

```bash
cd ~/code/my-project
fivexer-agent init --cwd . --access edit --allow-tools "WebSearch,WebFetch" --pass-env GITHUB_TOKEN
```

A task runs headless, so **nobody is there to approve a permission prompt, and anything the agent
would have asked about is refused.** For Claude Code and Codex with no `access` set, that means it
can read and answer, but not write a file, run a command or search the web. (Aider's preset already
accepts its edits; Goose, OpenCode and Cline follow their own config.) `access` says what it may
do without asking:

| `access`    | Meaning                                    | claude                                 | codex                                        | goose             |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `read-only` | look and answer, change nothing            | (its default)                          | `--sandbox read-only`                        | —                 |
| `edit`      | change files in the folder it runs in      | `--permission-mode acceptEdits`        | `--full-auto` (also runs commands, sandboxed) | —                 |
| `full`      | anything the person running the daemon can | `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`  | `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` | `GOOSE_MODE=auto` |

A level a CLI cannot express is refused — by `init`, and again when the daemon loads the config —
rather than approximated. OpenCode and Cline have no switch for it: set their permissions in their
own config, in the folder they run in. `allowTools` adds
individual tools on top, in the CLI's own syntax (Claude Code only); the allow lists in the
project's own `.claude/settings*.json` apply as well. `passEnv` lists the variables it may see, by
name — the child's environment is otherwise built from nothing.

**`full` is the person running the daemon, handed to whoever can send this worker work.** Tasks come
from the workspace, so keep `full` for a machine or container that exists for the agent. **`edit` in
a real project is close to it:** a task that can change files can change the project's scripts,
git hooks and the agent's own settings, which run later — so allow a command tool such as
`Bash(pnpm *)` only where that is acceptable, and remember that `WebFetch` can send out whatever
the agent can read. `doctor` prints what each profile may do. `init` writes `fivexer.agent.json`
into the folder it runs in; keep it out of version control or pass `--config`.

#### Changing it later

`init` refuses a profile that already exists — replacing one would orphan its worker — so what a
profile may do is changed with `profile` instead. It edits only the running settings (`cwd`,
`access`, `allowTools`, `passEnv`) and prints the result; restart the daemon for it to apply.

```bash
fivexer-agent profile research                                   # show
fivexer-agent profile research --add-tools "Bash(./scripts/publish.sh *)"
fivexer-agent profile research --remove-tools WebFetch --access edit
fivexer-agent profile research --add-claude-rules                # what you already allowed Claude Code
fivexer-agent profile research --pass-env none                   # "none" clears a list
```

`--add-claude-rules` copies `permissions.allow` from `.claude/settings.json` and
`settings.local.json` in the profile's folder and each folder above it, up to the repository root.
Claude Code itself reads only the folder it starts in, so approvals you gave it at a repository's
root do not reach an agent that runs in a sub-folder until they are copied. It lists the rules and
asks before saving (`--yes` adds them without asking, for a script), and only works for a profile
that runs in a folder (`workspace: "cwd"`) with an absolute `cwd`. Interactive `init` offers the
same rules in its tool checklist, unticked: they were approved with someone watching each call, and
here they would apply to every task anyone sends this worker.

After every run, the daemon logs the tool calls Claude Code refused, as rules, with the command that
allows them, so a profile missing one entry shows up in the log rather than only as an agent
apologising in a result you may never see.

Two different things are called "skills" and they are not the same. **Agent skills** live in that
directory and are what the agent can _do_. **Fivexer skills** live in the workspace catalog, are
attached to the worker, and decide which tasks it is _offered_. Keep them honest with each other —
an agent whose tags promise more than its tools deliver gets handed work it then has to reject.

### Declaring what the agent can do

Run by hand with a browser sign-in and no `--skills`, `init` works this out for you. It reads the
**names** of the agent's own MCP servers and skills (Claude Code: `~/.claude.json`, the agent home's
`.mcp.json` and `.claude/skills/`, `~/.claude/skills/`; Codex: `~/.codex/config.toml`,
`~/.codex/skills/`; OpenCode: `opencode.json`) — never a server's command, URL, env or headers. It can
also ask the agent once what it can do (it runs in its home with the usual environment allowlist, up
to two minutes). Then it lists suggested skills; Enter accepts them all, `1,3` keeps only those,
`Web research:4` adds one, `none` keeps none. Only the names you accept are sent, and it asks for the
worker's name in 5xer last. `--no-look` skips all of it; `--skills`, a join link, an API key or
`--yes` never trigger it.

Name each capability the way a person would, by catalog id, skill key or plain name, with a level
from 1 (novice) to 5 (expert):

```bash
fivexer-agent init --executor claude --tags seo --skills "SEO audit:4, web research"
```

or in the profile:

```json
"skills": [
  { "skill": "SEO audit", "level": 4 },
  { "skill": "translation", "name": "Translation", "description": "English and Estonian", "level": 3 }
]
```

Registration matches each one to the workspace catalog by id, then key, then name, so `SEO audit`
and `seo-audit` land on the same skill rather than two that never meet. What happens to a skill the
catalog does not have depends on the credential:

- **Browser sign-in or a workspace key**: the skill is added to the catalog for the next agent or
  person to reuse.
- **Join link**: the worker holds only its own session, and inventing a catalog skill is an
  operator's decision, so it claims the ones that exist and warns about the rest. Skills the worker
  already holds, from an operator or the link, are kept.

A skill's level counts twice: as a hard gate against a task's `requiredSkills`, and in ranking, so a
level-5 agent is offered the work ahead of a level-3 one.

Declared skills are re-stated from the worker's own session every time the daemon starts, so a
config edit takes effect on the next start, and an operator's later change to the *level* of a
declared skill is put back. Dates an operator set on a qualification and skills the operator added
are kept. `weightOverride` is applied only when a workspace key registers the worker; a worker
cannot set its own routing weight. `skillId` is still read as the older spelling of `skill`, and an
id is only ever reused, never created. In `--skills`, a trailing `:n` is always the level, so a key
that ends in a number needs its level written out: `cert:2:3`.

## Profiles

A profile **is** a Fivexer worker: its own id, tags, skills and backlog. Routing between profiles is
therefore done by the Fivexer matcher, on the same rules that route work to people — there is no
second dispatch layer on your host.

`~/.fivexer/config.json`, or `./fivexer.agent.json`, or `--config`. Strict JSON — no comments, no
trailing commas. `cwd` is where that agent's own MCP config and project state live:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```json
{
  "workspaceId": "ws_...",
  "profiles": [
    {
      "name": "research",
      "tags": ["agent", "research", "seo"],
      "skills": [{ "skill": "seo-audit", "level": 4 }],
      "executor": "claude",
      "cwd": "~/agents/research",
      "workspace": "cwd",
      "passEnv": ["BRAVE_API_KEY"],
      "timeoutMs": 900000
    },
    {
      "name": "dev",
      "tags": ["agent", "dev"],
      "executor": "opencode",
      "workspace": "worktree",
      "repo": "~/src/my-service",
      "concurrency": 2
    }
  ]
}
```

`FIVEXER_WORKSPACE_ID`, `FIVEXER_BASE_URL`, `FIVEXER_API_KEY`, `FIVEXER_STATE_DIR` and
`FIVEXER_POLL_INTERVAL_MS` override the file, so one config can be pointed at staging.

A profile registered by a join link carries `"registration": "join"` and an empty `tags` list —
its routing lives in the console, and a second copy here would only diverge. One caveat worth
knowing: join links do not set a backlog size, so such a worker gets the workspace default rather
than the profile's `concurrency`. The daemon still runs no more than `concurrency` tasks, but the
matcher may hand it more, and the surplus waits where nobody else can take it. Match the two, or
use the API-key path when the backlog matters.

### Profile options

| Field                 | Default               |                                                                                   |
| --------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`                | —                     | unique; also the suffix of the default worker id                                  |
| `registration`        | `api-key`             | `join` means the console owns tags; written by `init`/`join`                      |
| `workerId`            | `agent-<host>-<name>` | the host is in it because two machines sharing an id would fight over one backlog |
| `tags`                | —                     | required on the api-key path; a worker with no tags matches nothing, silently     |
| `skills`              | `[]`                  | `{ skill, level: 1–5, name?, description?, weightOverride? }`; see above         |
| `executor`            | —                     | a preset name, or `{ command, args, input }`                                      |
| `workspace`           | `scratch`             | `scratch` \| `cwd` \| `worktree`                                                  |
| `concurrency`         | `1`                   | also the worker's `maxBacklogSize`                                                |
| `passEnv`             | `[]`                  | environment variables the agent is allowed to see                                 |
| `access`              | —                     | `read-only` \| `edit` \| `full`; unset keeps the CLI's own defaults               |
| `allowTools`          | `[]`                  | tools allowed without asking, in the CLI's syntax (claude)                         |
| `timeoutMs`           | `900000`              | after this the process group is killed and the task requeued                      |
| `requireApprovalTags` | `[]`                  | tasks with any of these wait for an operator                                      |
| `progressIntervalMs`  | `0`                   | post a progress comment at most this often; `0` is off                            |

## Executors

Presets: `claude`, `codex`, `opencode`, `goose`, `aider`, `cline`. Or name a command yourself:

```json
{ "executor": { "command": "./scripts/handle-task.sh", "args": ["{{briefPath}}"], "input": "file" } }
```

`input` is how the brief reaches the process — `stdin`, `file` (path at `{{briefPath}}`), or
`inline` (substituted at `{{brief}}`). `{{resultPath}}`, `{{runDir}}` and `{{taskId}}` also
substitute. No shell is involved, so quoting inside a task can never become argument structure.

Presets are a convenience, not a contract. If a preset's flags have drifted, it fails as "command
not found" or falls back to the exit code — never to a confident wrong answer.

## The result contract

Each task gets a directory under `~/.fivexer/runs/<taskId>/` holding `task.json`, `BRIEF.md`,
`output.log` and `state.json`. `BRIEF.md` is a markdown document — the task description is
GitHub-flavored markdown by platform convention and passes through verbatim. The brief tells the
agent to write `result.json`, and the path is also in `$FIVEXER_RESULT_FILE`:

```json
{
    "success": true,
    "summary": "One short paragraph — stored on the task, read first by a person.",
    "output": "The full deliverable. Posted to the task thread.",
    "data": { "anythingStructured": "for downstream workflow steps" }
}
```

If no file appears, the daemon falls back to the preset's structured stdout, and then to the exit
code with the tail of the log. That last tier works for any command at all, which is what makes the
whole thing vendor-neutral. With the `claude` preset, the final message becomes the deliverable and
its opening paragraph the summary — a long report is attached rather than cut to a summary.

### When results are not kept

A workspace decides, in the console, whether an agent's results are kept on the platform — for all
agents, or one by one — and the default is **no**: only the verdict is sent (done, or why it could
not be done). The daemon reads this before each task. When results are not kept it posts no progress
and no deliverable, and completes with the verdict alone; everything the agent produced stays in
`~/.fivexer/runs/<taskId>/` on your machine. The platform enforces it too: it keeps only the verdict of
a completion, refuses file uploads, and accepts only short notes (500 characters) on the thread from
such an agent.

A workspace can also keep results **for a while**: then the daemon sends the whole result — the
deliverable included — in the completion, posts nothing to the thread, and the platform keeps it
sealed until a set time after the task ends, when it is deleted for good.

### Runs

Every task the daemon works is recorded in an **agent run**. Before accepting, it joins the run the
task already belongs to (one a manager — an agent with a workspace key, or a person — created it in)
or, for a task that was in none, such as one filed in the console, opens a run named after the task.
The accept, the result and the completion are then recorded there, and the console shows the task as
part of that run. The run id reaches the agent as `$FIVEXER_RUN_ID` and in `BRIEF.md`, which asks it
to pass `runId` and a `why` when it hands follow-up work to Fivexer, so follow-ups land in the same
run. The platform closes a run opened this way once every task in it has finished; a run with a
manager is the manager's to finish. All of this is best effort: on a platform without portal runs
the work goes ahead off the record, as before.

`summary` and `output` are kept apart deliberately: the summary goes into the task's completion
payload, which lives on the assignment and is read on every queue operation, while the deliverable
goes to the task itself. An `output` that fits in one comment is posted as one; a longer one is
uploaded as a single `text/markdown` **task attachment** (named `<taskId>-output.md`, redacted like
everything that leaves the host) with a pointer comment naming the file — a reviewer downloads a
document instead of stitching numbered comments back together. Deployments without object storage,
older APIs, or a failing upload all degrade to the classic 4 KB comment chunks. The untruncated
copy always stays on your host.

When the requester attached a **result contract** to the task, `BRIEF.md` shows it under "What the
requester will accept": plain-language criteria and/or a JSON Schema that `data` must satisfy. The
platform enforces the schema at completion; if the run's `data` misses it, the daemon reports the
task as `success: false` with the reason instead of claiming a success that was refused.

## Three kinds of failure

The daemon reports them differently, because Fivexer treats them differently.

- **The agent ran and could not do the work** → the task is _completed_ with `success: false`.
  A real outcome: it can be routed onward, and the learning layer sees it.
- **Trouble on this host** — missing binary, timeout, shutdown → the task is _rejected_, with the
  reason on the thread first, while the thread is still writable. It requeues for someone else.
- **The agent runtime itself died** — a provider outage, dead credentials, an exhausted quota →
  also _rejected_. These exit non-zero like a real failure, so without telling them apart a
  provider having a bad afternoon would permanently close every task it touched. Only the tail of
  the output counts as evidence: a stack trace in the middle is a tool result, and often exactly
  what the agent was asked to investigate.

Kill the daemon mid-task and nothing strands: in-flight tasks are requeued, and anything it misses
is caught by the task's own escalation and SLA clocks. On restart it recovers accepted work, and
reports a result a previous run finished but never sent rather than doing it twice.

## Safety

The posture is _sandbox and review the outcome_: the agent runs unattended in a bounded
environment, and a person reviews the deliverable before acting on it.

- **A task never influences how the agent is spawned.** Command, args, working directory and
  environment come from your config alone. A task reaches the agent only as text, fenced in
  `BRIEF.md` with an explicit note that it is a request to act on rather than instructions about
  how the agent or the host should behave. A task is filed by whoever wanted the work.
- **The agent never sees the daemon's credentials.** The child environment is built from nothing:
  `PATH`, `HOME` and a few locale variables, plus exactly what `passEnv` names. Not the workspace
  API key, not the worker session token.
- **Credentials the agent prints are masked before they leave the host.** Summaries, deliverables,
  structured result data and progress comments all go through a redactor covering `NAME=value`,
  `--flag value`, `Authorization:` headers and the common token shapes. `output.log` is left
  unmasked on purpose: it is the local diagnostic copy, written `0600`, and a filter that runs over
  a stream cannot see a secret split across two chunks — so masking there would be both weaker and
  destructive of the one faithful record of what happened.
- **Runs can be held for a person.** `requireApprovalTags` posts a request to the task thread and
  waits for `yes <id>` from a console user or an API integration. Comments authored by _any_
  worker are ignored — which is what stops an agent approving itself, since the API derives comment
  authorship from the session rather than the request body.
- The whole process group is killed on timeout or shutdown, so subprocesses an agent spawned do not
  outlive the task.

## Credentials

Steady state is always the same: a `wt_` worker session that reaches only its own worker's queue,
rotating itself before expiry, cached `0600` under `~/.fivexer/credentials/` alongside a generated
PIN. The PIN is kept because it is the only way back once a refresh chain hits its absolute
ceiling — without it an unattended agent needs a human to re-provision it.

The setup paths differ only in how that session is first obtained:

- **Browser sign-in** (default when you are at the machine) — the standard native-app OAuth flow:
  a public client, PKCE, and a redirect to a loopback port only this machine can reach. The token
  it returns opens the workspace, so it is held just long enough to mint a single-use join link,
  spend it, and set the worker's backlog and shift — then dropped. It is never written anywhere.
  The link it opens only works on the machine running the command; over SSH, use a join link.
- **Join link** — the console owns the worker's tags. Declared skills are claimed from the catalog
  on every start, never added to it; anything the link or an operator set is kept. If the link required approval, the
  machine registers but stays off shift until an operator admits it; `doctor` says so rather than
  looking like an empty queue.
- **API key** — `FIVEXER_API_KEY` creates the worker record and sets its PIN, then is not needed
  again. Read from the environment; never written to the config file.

## Platforms

Node 20.12 or newer. The floor is not arbitrary: on Windows the executor has to
go through a shell for `.cmd` shims, and 20.12 is where Node's argument escaping
for those was fixed.

|             |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Linux**   | Developed and tested here. `service install` writes a systemd **user** unit.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **macOS**   | Same code paths as Linux. `service install` writes a launchd agent.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Windows** | Handled deliberately — `.cmd` shims, `taskkill /T` for the process tree, a Scheduled Task from `service install`, no console windows — but **not yet exercised on a Windows machine**. The per-platform decisions have tests that run everywhere; a real Windows run has not happened. Treat it as supported-but-unproven and please report what breaks. |

Two behaviours differ on Windows and are worth knowing about. `.cmd` shims are
spawned through a shell because Node requires it, so for those the "no shell is
involved" property above is provided by Node's own argument escaping rather than
by avoiding the shell entirely — prefer `"input": "stdin"` or `"file"` on
Windows if that distinction matters to you. And file modes (`0600` on
credentials and run directories) are a no-op there; the state directory relies
on the user profile's own permissions.

## Running in production

Use `service install` rather than a bare `run` in a terminal — it sets the
restart policy and gives the daemon enough time on shutdown to hand its
in-flight tasks back.

Install it globally first. `npx` unpacks into a cache npm eventually deletes, so
a unit pointing there works today and stops weeks later; `service install`
refuses to write one and tells you this.

```bash
npm install -g @fivexer/agent
fivexer-agent service install      # prints the enable command; does not run it
```

Upgrades are `npm install -g @fivexer/agent@latest` then a restart of the
service. Nothing in the run directory or credential cache changes format between
patch versions.

What to watch: the worker's shift state in the Fivexer console tells you whether
a host is present — the daemon goes on shift when it starts and off when it
stops cleanly. A crash skips the off-shift step, which is the one case where the
console can lag reality; the task's own escalation and SLA clocks are what
actually guarantee nothing strands.

## Shift state

Workers are created off shift, on the assumption a human turns themselves on at a portal. An agent
has no portal, so the daemon goes on shift when it starts and off shift when it stops cleanly —
which also means a stopped daemon reads as off shift in team presence, rather than "working"
forever. A crash skips the off-shift step; the task's own escalation and SLA clocks are what
actually guarantee nothing strands.

## Interactive mode

`fivexer-agent mcp` exposes the task lifecycle as MCP tools (`fivexer_next_task`, `fivexer_accept`,
`fivexer_complete`, `fivexer_reject`, `fivexer_comment`), so any MCP-capable client can pull its own
work with no executor configured at all:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "fivexer": { "command": "npx", "args": ["fivexer-agent", "mcp"] } } }
```

# Changelog

## 0.7.0 — 2026-10-17

**Agents read and keep the workspace's knowledge.** The MCP server (`fivexer-agent mcp`) lists the
knowledge tools beside the task tools — `find_knowledge`, `read_knowledge`, `save_knowledge`,
`patch_knowledge`, `link_knowledge`, `knowledge_attention`, `archive_knowledge`, `open_screen`,
`show_knowledge` — and `fivexer-agent mcp --knowledge` serves only those. When the daemon runs a task
with Claude Code it passes that server with `--mcp-config` (as `fivexer-knowledge`) and allows its
tools; a `read-only` profile gets only the read tools. The task brief says the tools are there.

An agent reads all of the workspace's knowledge and writes only graphs of its own (a graph it
creates is its own); a personal assistant sees only its own graphs. Deleting and sharing knowledge
stay with people in the console.

The server a task run uses signs in with a session of its own from the stored PIN, never writes the
credentials file, never registers anything, and logs out when the run ends. `--config` reaches it
through `FIVEXER_AGENT_CONFIG`.

**Registering with a workspace key now registers an agent.** The identity is created with
`agent: true`, and an agent registered before this release marks itself on start while its key is
still configured — that is what lets it use knowledge. An agent that joined with a link needs
nothing.

## 0.6.0 — 2026-10-12

**`fivexer-agent profile <name>` changes what a profile may do after setup.** `--access`,
`--allow-tools`, `--add-tools`, `--remove-tools`, `--cwd` and `--pass-env` edit the running
settings in place, checked the same way `init` checks them, without touching the worker id or
registration; with no flags it prints them, and `none` clears a list. `--add-claude-rules` lists the
allow rules already in the project's `.claude/settings*.json`, from the profile's folder up to the
repository root, and adds them on a yes (or `--yes`); and
interactive `init` now offers those rules (unticked) in its tool checklist. After each run the
daemon logs the tool calls Claude Code refused (`permission_denials`) as rules, with the command
that allows them — before, a missing allowlist entry was visible only in the agent's own summary.

**`init` is a keyboard-driven setup at a terminal.** Choices are lists you move through with the
arrow keys — which agent, where it works, what it may do — and tools, environment variables and
skills are checklists toggled with Space, each with a "something else…" entry for free text. The
agent's self-description and registration run behind a spinner, and the summary is shown in the
same frame. Ctrl-C at any question stops before anything is registered or written.

Environment variables are offered by name from those set in the shell that look like credentials
(`*_API_KEY`, `*_TOKEN`, …), none ticked by default; values are never read. Claude Code's and the
editor's own session variables are not offered.

Nothing changes for scripts: without a terminal (a pipe, `--yes`, CI) every question is one line of
text as before, and flags still skip the question entirely. Answers there accept a value, its
number in the list, or its label. Built on `@clack/prompts`, loaded only by `init`.

## 0.5.0 — 2026-10-12

**An agent can work like it does for you, not only in an empty home.** Until now every profile
`init` or `join` wrote ran in `~/.fivexer/agents/<profile>` with no environment variables and the
agent CLI's default permissions. Headless, with nobody to answer a permission prompt, that meant an
agent could answer in text but not write a file (including its own `result.json`), search the web
or run a command, and never saw a project's skills, instructions or MCP servers. Three profile
settings change that, each a flag on `init` and `join` and a question when `init` has someone at
the keyboard (including the console's one-line join command):

- `--cwd <dir>` / `cwd` — run tasks in that folder. `init` offers the folder it was started in
  (yes by default inside a project). Agent-home files are never scaffolded into it.
- `--access read-only|edit|full` / `access` — what it may do without asking, in the same words
  for every agent. Each preset turns it into its own flags: Claude Code permission modes, Codex
  sandbox modes (Codex `edit` also runs commands inside its sandbox), Goose `GOOSE_MODE=auto` (full
  only). A level a CLI cannot express is refused — by `init` and again when the config loads —
  never approximated. Interactive `init` suggests `edit` where the CLI has it, and otherwise leaves
  the CLI's own settings alone.
- `--allow-tools "WebSearch,Bash(pnpm *)"` / `allowTools` — extra tools allowed without asking,
  for a CLI with an allowlist (Claude Code).
- `--pass-env A,B` / `passEnv` — variable names the agent may see. Names, never values.

Nothing changes for an existing config: no `access` keeps the CLI's own defaults. `doctor` now
says what each profile may do. `edit` in a real project can reach code execution (scripts, hooks,
the agent's own settings); the README says so.

**Presets:** `claude` adds `--add-dir {{runDir}}`, so an edit-allowed run can write `result.json`
outside the folder it works in. `codex` adds `--skip-git-repo-check`, without which `codex exec`
refuses to start in an agent home or a scratch directory. `ExecutorSpec` takes an optional `env`
of fixed variables; `executorFor(profile)` returns the spec a profile actually runs.

## 0.4.0 — 2026-10-12

**`init` suggests the agent's skills itself.** On a browser sign-in with nobody passing `--skills`,
it reads the names (only) of the agent's MCP servers and skills, can ask the agent once to describe
what it does, and offers the result as a numbered list to accept, trim or add to — plus a suggested
worker name. `--no-look` turns it off.

**An agent says what it can do in plain words, and the catalog keeps up.** A profile's `skills`
now take `{ skill, level }`, where `skill` is a catalog id, a skill key or a name (`"SEO audit"`),
and `init --skills "SEO audit:4, web research"` writes them. Registration matches each one to the
workspace catalog by id, then key, then name. A workspace key or a browser sign-in adds a skill
the catalog lacks; a join-link worker claims existing skills from its own session and is told
which are missing. Skills are re-stated on every start, keeping what an operator set.

**Typing change:** `AgentConfig.skills` is `SkillInput[]` and `ProfileConfig.skills` is
`DeclaredSkill[]`; `SkillAssignment` now comes from `worker/skill-catalog`. Config files and code
that pass `{ skillId, level }` keep working, read as a declaration by id.

## 0.3.0

**A crashed daemon no longer reads as "available" forever.** Going on shift now
declares a liveness contract (`staleAfterMs`, 5× the poll interval with a
two-minute floor), and the platform's shift janitor clocks the worker out and
pauses routing once it has been silent well past that. Until now the only clean
way off shift was `standDown()` on an orderly shutdown, so a killed process — or
a host that lost power — sat in team presence as working, with the SLA and
escalation clocks as the only thing recirculating its work. Liveness rides on
the polls the daemon already makes; there is no heartbeat call and no extra
traffic. The window is deliberately generous: a slow tick or a brief network
wobble must never clock a live daemon out. Requires `@fivexer/sdk` ≥ 0.27.0 and
a platform running the shift janitor; against anything older the field is
ignored and behaviour is unchanged.

## 0.2.0

**A long deliverable is now handed over as a file, not a comment stream.** When
a run's output does not fit in one comment, the agent uploads it as a single
`text/markdown` task attachment — bytes go straight to the platform's object
storage via a presigned PUT — and posts one pointer comment naming the file and
its size. A reviewer downloads a document instead of stitching up to eight
numbered chunks back together. The content is redacted before it leaves the
host, exactly like comments; short outputs stay plain comments.

**Nothing about this can strand a task.** A deployment without object storage
(501), an older API without the portal attachment routes (404), or a storage
PUT that keeps failing (retried once) all degrade to the chunked-comment
delivery this package has always done, with a warning on stderr. Requires the
platform's worker-plane attachment routes and `@fivexer/sdk` ≥ 0.26.0 to take
the file path; against anything older the behaviour is unchanged.

## 0.1.2

**`init` talked to a host that does not exist.** The default API root was
`https://api.fivexer.com`, which has no DNS record; the live one is
`https://api.5xer.com`. Every first run with no `--base-url` ended at
`fivexer: fetch failed`. The same address was in the SDK and Expo README
examples, so it was copy-pasteable too.

**A sign-in that fails now offers the join path instead of giving up.** You have
already chosen a profile name and an agent by that point, and a browser that
cannot get through — a headless host, a proxy, a self-hosted deployment at
another address — is a reason to offer the other door, not to throw the answers
away. Non-interactive runs still fail outright, since there is nothing there to
ask.

**Network failures name the host.** Node reports them all as `fetch failed` and
puts the part worth reading in the cause; both the sign-in and the top-level
error handler now say which address and whether DNS or the connection was the
problem.

## 0.1.1

Everything here is a fix to something 0.1.0 got wrong or left out. Nothing in
the task lifecycle changed, so an existing config keeps working as-is.

**`service install` no longer writes a unit that breaks later.** Run through
`npx`, it pointed the unit at the npx cache — a directory npm eventually
deletes, so the service worked on the day it was set up and then stopped for no
visible reason. It now refuses, with the global-install command to run instead,
or writes a unit pinned to `npx @fivexer/agent@<version>` under `--allow-npx`.

**Windows.** Several things were wrong and would have failed on first use:

- npm-installed CLIs on Windows are `.cmd` shims, which Node refuses to spawn
  without a shell — every preset would have failed with `ENOENT`. The executor
  now resolves the command first and uses a shell only for those shims. Node
  `>=20.12` is required, since that is where Node's argument escaping for them
  was fixed.
- Killing a timed-out run signalled a negative pid, which does nothing on
  Windows: an agent's subprocesses outlived the task and kept working on it.
  Now uses `taskkill /T`.
- `where` prints CRLF, so a resolved path carried a trailing `\r` and failed to
  spawn with a confusing error.
- `service install` wrote a systemd unit — a file nothing on Windows reads. It
  now writes a Scheduled Task, with the execution time limit removed so a worker
  is not stopped after three days.
- Child processes no longer pop up a console window.

**Added.** `--version` / `fivexer-agent version`, and `./package.json` is
exposed in `exports` so tooling can read the manifest.

## 0.1.0

First release. A host-side daemon that registers a local AI agent CLI as a
Fivexer worker, runs tasks it is routed, and reports results back.

- Vendor-neutral by construction: spawns a command and reads a `result.json`,
  falling back to structured stdout and then the exit code. A `#!/bin/sh`
  script is a first-class executor.
- Profiles, each registering as its own worker, so routing stays the matcher's
  job.
- Setup by browser sign-in, join link, or API key — none of which leaves a
  long-lived workspace credential on the host.
- Three failure kinds reported distinctly: work that could not be done, trouble
  on this host, and an agent runtime that died.
- Credentials the agent prints are masked before anything is published.
